newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Fran pounds U.S. east coast, seven die.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Fran pounds U.S. east coast, seven die.

text.p: Hurricane Fran pounded the southeast United States on Friday before roaring inland, claiming at least seven lives and plunging towns along a 100-mile (160 km) stretch of the Carolina coast into darkness.
Winds of up to 120 mph (193 kph) snapped power lines, tossed trees into houses and onto highways and caused extensive damage in some areas of North and South Carolina.
The National Hurricane Centre warned that heavy rains could lead to flooding and there was the potential for serious floods inland.
There was also a possibility of isolated tornadoes over parts of eastern North Carolina and central and southeastern Virginia, the Miami-based hurricane centre said.
At 1 a.m. EDT (0500 GMT), the storm's centre was 20 miles (32 km) east of Fayetteville in North Carolina and was moving north north-west.
Fran was expected to continue moving northwards throughout Friday morning, which would put its centre over eastern North Carolina and Virginia later in the day.

At least seven deaths were linked to Fran. Two people were killed south of Raleigh when their vehicle struck a tree that had fallen across a highway, said Frank Cope, public information officer for Wake county in North Carolina.
In North Carolina's Onslow county, an 18-year-old woman died on Thursday night when a tree toppled by hurricane-force winds fell onto her mobile home, emergency officials said.

Two people were killed in Johnston county when a tree fell on their home and a Durham county fireman was killed responding to an emergency call, said a spokesman for North Carolina's emergency management team.
In South Carolina, an elderly woman died on a rain-slicked highway when she lost control of her car and crashed into a tree, the state highway patrol said.
North Carolina Governor Jim Hunt said the hurricane had caused "very serious damage" in his state.

"There are 5-10 feet (1.524 metres to 3.048 metres) of water on some of those roads right on the coast," Hunt said from the state's emergency management centre. "There are a lot of trees down and power is out in many, many counties.

In the small North Carolina town of Southport, officials also said damage had been severe. "We've got a lot of destruction," said Steve Robbins, a Southport Police Department dispatcher. "There are a lot of buildings down, demolished. It's really bad down here.
"It was almost like a movie," Robbins said, when the eye passed over the small town. "The whole city was black. It was like a horror movie."

In Raleigh, a city almost 100 miles inland, damage was extensive from fallen trees and high winds. "Things are so bad we are urging people not to even go to shelters anymore because of the fallen trees," said Cope. "It's more dangerous to get on the highways than to stay home."
All along the coast of North and South Carolina, nuclear power reactors were shut, shops and bridges closed and homes boarded up as people waited out the storm.
About 200,000 residents evacuated low-lying areas and sought refuge in motels, stayed with friends or went to Red Cross shelters.

Hurricane warnings were in effect from Camp Lejeune, North Carolina to the North Carolina/Virginia border. A tropical storm warning continued northward from that border to Chincoteague, Virginia, and also for the lower Chesapeake Bay.
Virginia started bracing for the worst of Fran's fury on Friday. A state of emergency was declared and the National Guard placed on alert.

In South Carolina, which missed the worst of Fran's force, at least 58,700 customers had no power in the Myrtle Beach area. An additional 10,000 homes on the beach area known as "the Grand Strand" were also left in the dark after palm trees felled power lines.

Emergency officials urged residents to remain in their homes or shelters until well after dawn, when crews would have had a chance to assess the damage. South Carolina officials said the state could lose about $8 million a day in tourist revenue because of the hurricane.
